method: All nine printed pages read visually at 2x from the supplied Part 1 PDF, with explicit local traversals recorded below. Ordered source blocks include every instructional list/table row, causal chain, and named diagram element. Contiguous labels can share an item; no later source block is pulled forward. Numeric nephron labels are read with their printed legend across p717-718. Source inconsistencies are not silently taught as clinical facts. Headers, timestamps, footer and blank Active space are excluded.
caveats: p717: bladder/cloaca primitive-rectum parenthesis and cephalic-for-phallic wording are flagged; vesico-ureteric is clarified as vesicourethral. The numbered nephron sketch is schematic and macula densa is not a separate long tubular segment.
p718: renal-failure tree is a teaching subset, not exhaustive AKI differential or stand-alone diagnostic criteria.

p719: all-ions and kidney-only phosphorus wording are oversimplifications. The upper basolateral Na/H arrows conflict with the lower apical exchanger sketch and canonical physiology; flagged explicitly.

p720: Fanconi and isolated proximal RTA are not synonyms in all cases. No CKD risk is an unsafe universal claim. Urine pH 4-4.5 and bicarbonate 16-18 are source descriptions, not mandatory diagnostic values or proof of no acidosis.

p721: AIP wording and membrane-adjacent receptor symbol are schematic; ENaC is not an H/K/water exchanger. ROMK is a potassium channel; SOMK is a nonstandard printed label with no invented expansion. PHA fibrosis/drug mechanisms are simplified; vesico-urethral reflux is clarified as vesicoureteral reflux.

p722: beta-cell basolateral anion-exchanger sketch is flagged against canonical H-ATPase physiology; AR pump groupings are source-specific. Toluene is an exposure, not medication. Type-III osteoporosis is corrected explicitly to classic CA-II-deficiency osteopetrosis; outdated disability terminology replaced.

p723: AR/M>F/normal-RFT common-features cell is not universal and conflicts with earlier AD/acquired branches. Comparison severity and urine-solute patterns are simplified. Bicarbonate doses are source teaching ranges, not prescriptions. Countercurrent exchange is primarily vasa recta function, not a distinct unnamed-cell lineage. Urine gap is an imperfect NH4 surrogate, especially outside classic distal RTA.

p724: Na/K pump 3K label conflicts with 3Na/2K stoichiometry. TALH H2O paracellular arrow conflicts with water impermeability. Hypomagnesuria-to-hypomagnesemia wording is cautioned. Older Bartter type-V calcium-sensing-receptor classification and percentages remain source-qualified; indomethacin requires specialist supervision.

p725: TRMP6/ileum/100% chain is not an obligatory second ileal defect in Gitelman. No hypocalciuria conflicts with typical low urine Ca and the table; explicitly corrected. Salt-water retention table label conflicts with salt wasting; Gitelman low magnesium row is ambiguous versus preceding 100% claim.

pages.traversal: Renal-compartment tree left-to-right; embryology list top-to-bottom, completing each numbered entry and its sub-bullets. Then adjacent nephron figure: cortex/medullary zones, ray and loop labels; numbered structures are covered with their printed legend below and its continuation on p718. Excretory tree: origin, then numbered 1–8, completing PT, IT and DT branches. No return to an earlier branch. Decorative headings/timestamps/blank Active space excluded.

elements.source: The renal compartment tree allocates 85% to tubules/interstitium, 10% to glomeruli and 5% to vessels.
Embryology entry 1 prints bladder: cloaca (primitive rectum); the parenthesis is misleading.
The trigone exception is linked to the mesonephric duct and labelled mesodermal.
Prostate: primitive urogenital sinus.
Prostatic urethra up to the ejaculatory-duct opening: vesico-ureteric canal in the scan.
Membranous urethra and remaining prostatic urethra: pelvic part of definitive urogenital sinus.
Spongy urethra is assigned to cephalic part of urogenital sinus in this scan; this conflicts with phallic terminology.
Rectum: primitive rectum derived from cloaca.
Anal canal up to the pectinate line: cloaca; below the line: anal pit.
Nephron figure labels cortex above the outer and inner medulla.
The figure divides outer medulla into outer stripe and inner stripe.
The medullary ray label points to straight tubular structures extending into cortex.
Long-loop nephron enters inner medulla; short-loop nephron turns higher in the outer-medullary region.
The excretory part is traced to nephrogenic cord from the urogenital ridge.
Number 1: glomerulus plus Bowman's capsule form the renal corpuscle.
Proximal tubule branches into proximal convoluted and proximal straight tubules.
Number 2: proximal convoluted tubule, pars convoluta, S1 and S2.
Number 3: proximal straight tubule, pars recta, S3.
Intermediate tubule comprises numbered thin descending (4) and thin ascending (5) limbs.
Number 6: thick ascending limb, also called distal straight tubule.
Number 7: distal convoluted tubule, the other distal-tubule branch.
Number 8 is labelled macula densa in the source legend; the figure/legend correspondence is schematic.

pages.traversal: Collecting legend 9–12 top-to-bottom, then origin tree from collecting structures through ureteric bud, mesonephric duct and intermediate mesoderm. Nephron table row-by-row, left cell then right. Renal-failure flowchart depth-first: non-CKD → hours-to-days AKI → tubular injury then interstitial nephritis → extrarenal pre/postrenal branches; next days-to-weeks branch; finally CKD branch. All children completed before returning to the parent split.

elements.source: Collecting legend 9: connecting tubule (CT).
Collecting legend 10, 11, 12: cortical, outer medullary and inner medullary collecting ducts.
The collecting-part bracket lists CT, CD, ureter, pelvis and calyces.
Collecting-part origin: epithelium of ureteric bud.
Ureteric bud derives from mesonephric duct, which derives from intermediate mesoderm.
The table calls cortical nephrons short-looped and juxtamedullary nephrons long-looped.
Cortical nephrons make up 85%; juxtamedullary nephrons 15%.
The short-loop tip is described at the outer/inner medullary junction; the long-loop tip lies inside inner medulla.
Cortical nephrons have a lesser role in concentration; juxtamedullary nephrons have a major role.
The non-CKD branch labels renal failure over hours to days as acute kidney injury.
AKI divides into tubulointerstitial causes and causes outside the kidney.
Acute tubular necrosis/tubular injury is the first tubulointerstitial branch.
The book identifies ischemia as the most common cause of acute tubular injury.
The most commonly affected site is PST, proximal straight tubule.
Acute interstitial nephritis is paired with hypersensitivity reaction.
Causes outside the kidney divide into pre-renal and post-renal branches.
The days-to-weeks branch is rapidly progressive renal failure.
CKD is expanded as chronic kidney disease and linked to decreased functional nephron number.

pages.traversal: Opening PCT statement; transporter tree depth-first: secondary active symport list 1–3 then antiport, then passive branch. Phosphate-loss arrow chain. Upper cell: luminal symports top-to-bottom, basolateral label; intercellular passive arrow and solute list. Lower cell: luminal Na/H exchange → luminal bicarbonate/CA-IV cycle → CO2 entry → intracellular CA-II → basolateral bicarbonate exit. Final magnesium note last.

elements.source: The PCT introductory line says maximum reabsorption of all ions except magnesium; this is a teaching simplification.
PCT transporter tree: secondary active transport includes symport and antiport.
Symport 1: sodium-dependent amino-acid transporter.
Symport 2: sodium-dependent glucose transporter, SGLT-2.
Symport 3: sodium-dependent phosphate transporter type II.
The secondary active antiport is sodium–hydrogen exchange.
Passive transport is paracellular, on the boundary between two cells.
The phosphorus sentence says only handled in kidney; the arrow chain is PCT damage → phosphorus loss → rickets.
Upper PCT figure luminal symports carry Na with amino acids, glucose and phosphate.
Upper PCT figure places Na/H arrows on its basolateral side; this is an apparent diagram error.
Passive intercellular arrow lists H2O, Ca2+, Na+, Mg2+ and K+.
Lower PCT cell: luminal Na/H exchange brings sodium in and secretes hydrogen.
Luminal hydrogen combines with bicarbonate to form carbonic acid.
Luminal carbonic anhydrase IV converts carbonic acid to water and carbon dioxide.
The carbon-dioxide arrow crosses from lumen into the PCT cell.
Intracellular carbonic anhydrase II forms carbonic acid from water and carbon dioxide.
Intracellular carbonic acid supplies recycled H+ and bicarbonate exiting basolaterally.
The closing note locates maximum magnesium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb.

pages.traversal: Title and inherited/acquired comparison, then complete inherited column top-to-bottom before acquired column. Drug-exception note. Cardinal manifestations 1–6, finishing every sub-bullet and each causal arrow before moving on. Other features: left column hypouricemia, hypocarnitinemia, polyuria; right column dehydration then minimal proteinuria.

elements.source: The title equates global PCT dysfunction with Fanconi syndrome/type-2/proximal RTA; the equivalence is incomplete.
The source places inherited causes much more prominently than acquired causes.
Cystinosis is labelled the most common childhood cause.
Cystinosis is labelled autosomal recessive.
Galactosemia is the next inherited Fanconi cause.
Wilson disease is marked most common in adolescents.
Drugs are labelled the most common acquired cause in adults.
The adult drug list, first three entries: ifosfamide, tenofovir, valproate.
The final drug entries are outdated tetracycline and cisplatin.
Multiple myeloma is marked most common in the elderly.
Acetazolamide and topiramate cause acidosis without generalised PCT dysfunction by inhibiting bicarbonate reabsorption.
Cardinal feature 1: phosphorus loss causes renal rickets.
Cardinal feature 2 prints normal RFT, very minimal proteinuria and no CKD risk; the final claim is unsafe as a universal rule.
Cardinal feature 3: euglycemic glycosuria.
Cardinal feature 4: amino-acid loss in urine causes wasting/growth retardation.
Cardinal feature 5: urinary bicarbonate loss causes normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
The anion gap range printed is 8–12 mEq/L.
NAGMA is also called hyperchloremic acidosis.
The important sub-bullet says urine acidification remains normal, mainly through intercalated cells.
The source prints normal urine pH 4–4.5 under proximal RTA; this is not a universal normal range.
The source gives bicarbonate 16–18 mEq with the phrase no significant acidosis.
Salt/water depletion → secondary RAAS activation → increased aldosterone → K wasting → hypokalemia.
Other feature: hypouricemia.
Other feature: hypocarnitinemia.
Other feature: polyuria.
Other feature: dehydration.
Other feature: minimal proteinuria.

pages.traversal: Cell-type tree left-to-right. P-cell figure: luminal and basolateral orientation, then zona glomerulosa → aldosterone/receptor → AIP → ENaC arrows, then ROMK/SOMK labels; excess-aldosterone triad below. RTA-IV definition and two hyperkalemia lines. Types depth-first: complete true hypoaldosteronism low-renin branch including diabetic sub-bullets, then high-renin branch; complete acquired pseudo branch before inherited PHA types.

elements.source: The CCD cell-type tree lists P-cell, alpha-intercalated, beta-intercalated and unnamed cell.
The P-cell figure marks luminal membrane left and basolateral membrane right.
Zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone, which binds the depicted aldosterone receptor.
Aldosterone acts via a receptor and AIP, expanded in the source as aldosterone inducing protein.
AIP positively stimulates ENaC; the sketch couples luminal sodium/water entry to it.
The lower luminal P-cell figure labels ROMK and SOMK with K/H secretion arrows.
Excess aldosterone gives hypertension, metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia, bracketed as Conn syndrome.
The pathology heading links hypoaldosteronism to type-IV RTA.
The first RTA-IV descriptor is hyperkalemia without renal failure.
The second descriptor is hyperkalemia disproportionate to the degree and duration of renal failure.
The low-renin true-hypoaldosteronism branch has reduced renin and reduced aldosterone.
Low-renin cause 1: NSAIDs.
Low-renin cause 2: beta-blockers.
Low-renin cause 3: aliskiren, a direct renin inhibitor.
Low-renin cause 4: diabetes, with autonomic neuropathy and beta-1 receptor dysfunction.
The diabetes subdiagram shows impaired prorenin-to-renin conversion.
High-renin hypoaldosteronism means increased renin with reduced aldosterone.
High-renin cause 1: adrenal insufficiency/Addison disease.
High-renin drug list starts with ACE inhibitors and ARBs.
The source groups heparin and ketoconazole under aldosterone-synthesis inhibition.
Acquired pseudo-hypoaldosteronism first lists chronic tubulointerstitial fibrosis from vesicourethral reflux and obstructive nephropathy.
The next acquired PHA bullet names calcineurin inhibitors under drugs producing fibrosis.
Aldosterone receptor blockers: spironolactone and eplerenone.
ENaC channel blockers: amiloride and triamterene.
Trimethoprim is compared structurally to triamterene in the source.
Pentamidine is the final acquired drug listed.
Inherited pseudo-hypoaldosteronism branches are PHA type 1 and type 2.

pages.traversal: Top renin list, with inhibitory NSAID/beta-blocker side arrows. Alpha-cell diagram luminal pumps then intracellular enzyme and legend; beta-cell diagram luminal pendrin then basolateral anion label/legend. Distal-RTA tree: inherited AD branch then AR branch, acquired causes in listed order. Clinical manifestations lower-left top-to-bottom including calcium subbranches and salt-loss cascade, then lower-right type-III note. Source errors kept local and flagged.

elements.source: Renin stimulators: prostaglandins, beta-1 receptors and renal hypoperfusion.
The side arrows show NSAIDs inhibiting prostaglandin signalling and beta-blockers inhibiting beta-1 signalling.
Alpha-intercalated-cell black luminal symbol is H/K ATPase: H secreted and K taken into cell.
The alpha-cell red luminal symbol is H ATPase.
The alpha-cell intracellular enzyme is carbonic anhydrase II.
Beta-cell luminal pendrin exchanges bicarbonate outward for chloride inward.
The beta-cell basolateral red symbol is called anion exchanger in the scan; its literal physiology needs qualification.
Inherited distal-RTA AD branch: anion-exchanger defect.
Inherited distal-RTA AR branch: H ATPase or H/K ATPase defect.
The inherited AR branch may present with sensorineural hearing loss.
Acquired distal RTA: Sjogren syndrome is marked most common.
Rare acquired agents listed are amphotericin B and toluene.
Rare acquired diseases listed are primary biliary cirrhosis and SLE.
Clinical manifestations 1 and 2: most common in children and normal RFT.
Inability to acidify urine is specified as pH above 5.5 for three consecutive days.
Significant distal-RTA NAGMA: bicarbonate 10–12 mEq/L.
The calcium branch runs bone calcium release to hypercalciuria.
Hypercalciuria subbranch 1: calcium-phosphate stone formation.
Hypercalciuria subbranch 2: medullary nephrocalcinosis.
Hypercalciuria subbranch 3: renal rickets.
Hypocitraturia leads to stones.
Salt/water wasting → reduced renal perfusion → secondary hyperaldosteronism → hypokalemia.
Type-III RTA note: carbonic anhydrase II defect.
The type-III feature list prints osteoporosis, which conflicts with the classic CA-II-deficiency osteopetrosis association.
Type-III features continue with intellectual disability and cerebral calcification.

pages.traversal: Comparison table row-by-row from common features through dose; read each row distal column then proximal column, completing all bullets within the defect row. Unnamed-cell heading and four lines in order. Urine-gap paragraph then electroneutrality equation, rearranged equation, positive branch before negative branch; adjacent ammonium diagram follows last.

elements.source: The table common-features cell lists inherited cause (M>F), autosomal recessive and normal RFT.
Defect-site row: distal alpha-intercalated cell; proximal global PCT dysfunction.
Distal defect row lists H ATPase, H/K ATPase and anion exchanger.
Proximal defect row lists symport, antiport and passive paracellular transport.
Phosphorus-loss row: no in distal; significant in proximal.
Calcium-loss row: significant in distal; not present in proximal.
Rickets row: calcium loss in distal versus phosphorus loss in proximal.
NAGMA row: severe distal; mild proximal.
Secondary hyperaldosteronism row: severe distal, mild proximal.
Hypokalemia row: severe distal, mild proximal.
Aminoaciduria row: no in distal; significant in proximal.
Hypocitraturia row: present distal, absent proximal.
Bicarbonate-treatment row: distal 2–4 mEq/kg/day; proximal 10–15 mEq/kg/day.
Unnamed-cell hormone: ADH.
Unnamed-cell channel protein: aquaporin.
The source lists countercurrent exchanger as an unnamed-cell function; the attribution is misleading.
The next function is reabsorption of free water.
Urine anion gap is used here to distinguish RTA, mainly type 1, from VIPoma.
Electroneutrality: Na + K + unmeasured cations = Cl + unmeasured anions.
Rearranged urine gap: Na + K − Cl = unmeasured anions − unmeasured cations.
A positive gap points toward RTA in the source branch.
A negative gap points toward VIPoma in the second branch.
The diagram shows H combining with NH3 to form NH4, an unmeasured cation; NH4 is reduced in RTA.

pages.traversal: TALH physiology diagram: labelled luminal side, numbered 1 cotransport then 2 K recycling, basolateral pump above numbered 3 chloride/4 barttin, then paracellular claudin arrow. Bartter pathology bullets and causal chain, all five consequence bullets. Types tree left-to-right, completing each branch I–V before the next. Indomethacin/PG/RAS treatment arrows last.

elements.source: The section is the thick ascending limb of Henle, TALH.
Luminal transporter 1 brings Na, K and two Cl into the TALH cell.
Luminal transporter 2 is ROMK recycling potassium to create lumen electropositivity.
The basolateral pump drawing labels 3K and 3Na; equal stoichiometry is a source error.
Basolateral label 3: ClCKB chloride channel; label 4: Barttin.
The intercellular arrow labels claudin-mediated passive paracellular transport of H2O and calcium/magnesium.
Bartter heading: autosomal recessive, with a Na/K/2Cl channel defect.
The first causal arrow links the transport defect to severe salt wasting.
Salt wasting produces polyuria and failure to thrive.
Secondary RAAS activation is labelled prostaglandin mediated.
The cascade next shows urinary K and H loss.
The first two consequence bullets are hypokalemia and alkalosis.
Hypercalciuria is linked to renal stones.
The scan prints hypomagnesuria leading to hypomagnesemia in 20%; the urinary direction is inconsistent with renal Mg wasting.
The final Bartter consequence bullet is normal to low blood pressure.
Type I is marked most common and associated with children and maternal polyhydramnios.
Type II branch: children.
Type III is called classical and linked to adult presentation.
Type IV may present with sensorineural hearing loss.
The type-V source branch specifies autosomal-dominant inheritance.
The type-V source defect is calcium-sensing receptor dysfunction with hypocalcemia.
Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin-mediated secondary RAS activation in the treatment diagram.

pages.traversal: DCT figure: luminal Na/Cl arrows, basolateral upper Cl arrow then lower Na/K arrows. Gitelman inheritance/age/defect followed by clinical bullets and their causal arrows top-to-bottom, preserving apparent errors as explicit caveats; hypercalciuria note next. Bartter/Gitelman comparison row-by-row, left then right, through final magnesium row. No comparisons are pulled ahead of the prose.

elements.source: DCT luminal physiology shows Na/Cl symport into the cell.
The DCT diagram shows basolateral chloride exit above the sodium/potassium exchange arrows.
Gitelman syndrome is listed as autosomal recessive.
The source lists adults beneath Gitelman syndrome.
Gitelman defect: Na/Cl symport.
The first Gitelman clinical bullet is normal RFT.
Less salt/water depletion activates secondary RAAS and leads to mild hypokalemia, alkalosis, polyuria and failure to thrive.
The source links DCT Na/Cl defect to TRMP6 defect in ileum, impaired Mg absorption and 100% hypomagnesemia; this is not an established obligatory second defect.
The scan prints no hypocalciuria (no stones), contradicting its low-urine-calcium table and classic Gitelman phenotype.
The following source bullet says no hypermagnesemia.
The hypercalciuria note gives urinary calcium above 4 mg/kg/day.
Comparison row polyuria: more in Bartter, less in Gitelman.
Comparison row polydipsia: more in Bartter, less in Gitelman.
Comparison row dehydration: more in Bartter, less in Gitelman.
Comparison row tetany: less in Bartter, more in Gitelman.
Comparison row growth retardation: more in Bartter, less in Gitelman.
The table row prints salt water retention: more Bartter, less Gitelman, conflicting with both salt-wasting descriptions.
Comparison row urine calcium: more Bartter, less Gitelman.
Comparison row nephrocalcinosis: more Bartter, less Gitelman.
Final hypomagnesemia row: Bartter in 20% (type V), Gitelman low; the latter is ambiguous against the preceding 100% assertion.
